sections.skill: Explain why code that looks right can be wrong and how to check it

questions.prompt: Why can generated code be wrong even when it looks neat?

choices.text: The model predicts likely code without proving it
Because computers cannot run neat code
Because comments stop code from running
Because neat code is always wrong, and only messy code can actually work correctly

questions.correct_answer: The model predicts likely code without proving it
questions.intro: AI-generated code often LOOKS right: neat layout, sensible names, helpful comments. It can still be WRONG, because the model predicts likely code rather than proving it correct. Common problems: logic that works for one example but not others, misunderstood requirements, missing cases such as an empty list, and calls to functions or settings that do not exist. To check code: read it and trace it, RUN it on several inputs whose correct answers you already know, and compare results. Passing one test does not prove the code is right.

sections.skill: Compare checking code with checking a calculator you built

questions.prompt: Why type 2 + 2 into a new calculator?

choices.text: Because 2 + 2 is the only problem that any calculator can ever solve correctly

questions.correct_answer: You already know the answer
questions.intro: Imagine you built a calculator and want to know if it works. You would not just admire the buttons. You would type problems you already know the answer to: 2 + 2, 10 - 3, 5 * 5. If one gives a wrong result, you know something is broken, even if the others were right. Generated code is like a new calculator: neat appearance proves nothing; known-answer tests do.

questions.prompt: The calculator gets 2 + 2 right but 5 * 5 wrong. Does it work?

questions.prompt: A tool explains its code "removes duplicates," but running it leaves duplicates. Which should you trust?

choices.text: The explanation, since the tool knows its own code better than any test that you could run
What the code actually does when run

questions.correct_answer: What the code actually does when run
questions.intro: Confident explanations make wrong code more convincing. A tool may describe what code "does" based on what it was supposed to do, not what it actually does. Comments can be wrong too. Trust behavior over descriptions: run it, and test the boundaries (the smallest, largest, empty and unusual inputs). When the code will affect money, safety, privacy or other people, have someone experienced review it before it is used.
